 Her Tax Refund Can Go Straight Into Her IRA, Split Across Up to Three Accounts, With One Extra Form
 Most filers send their spring refund straight to groceries and bills, but a single extra form buried in the tax code opens a door that almost nobody walks through.
 By David Beren 
 Published November 3, 2026, 10:29am ET · 4 min read 
 Life After Work desk. Editor: David Beren .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 IRS Form 8888 lets filers route a tax refund directly into a traditional IRA, Roth IRA, or SEP IRA across up to three accounts.
 Depositing $3,000 annually into an IRA for 30 years at 6% return could grow to approximately $237,175.
 A refund arriving after the April 15 due date is not a valid IRA contribution for that year, requiring an amended return.

 For many families, the federal tax refund lands in a checking account every spring and gets spent on groceries , bills, and other everyday costs within a few weeks. The tax return has an option that most filers never use. It lets a filer send that refund straight into an IRA, or split it across up to three accounts, by adding one extra form. The tool for putting a tax refund into an IRA is IRS Form 8888, a single page added to the return.
 One Page Turns a Refund Into a Retirement Contribution
 Form 8888, called Allocation of Refund , tells the IRS to deposit your refund (or part of it) directly into two or three accounts at a U.S. bank, mutual fund, brokerage firm, or credit union. The form’s instructions say an eligible account can be a traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA), Roth IRA, SEP IRA (but not a SIMPLE IRA). An IRA is a personal retirement account with tax breaks. The form also accepts health savings accounts and Coverdell education savings accounts. The amounts on its three lines must add up to the full refund shown on the return.
 Where the IRS Puts It in Writing
 The rule shows up in three official IRS documents. The Rev. December 2025 Form 8888 lists IRAs as eligible accounts. The Form 1040 instructions, revised February 2026, state that a refund “can be split and directly deposited into up to three different accounts in your name.” Publication 590-A says you can contribute by having a refund “paid directly to your traditional IRA or Roth IRA.” Under the tax code, an IRA can’t accept contributions above the annual limit (26 U.S.C. § 408(a)(1)).
 Who Qualifies and Who Gets Shut Out
 She needs earned income, which the IRS calls compensation. Publication 590-A says she can’t contribute in a year she doesn’t work unless she can claim taxable alimony, nontaxable combat pay, or military differential pay, or file a joint return with a spouse who has compensation. That last exception is the spousal IRA , which 24/7 Wall St. covered recently.
 For 2026, Roth IRA eligibility starts phasing out at modified AGI of $153,000 for single filers and ends at $168,000. For joint filers, the range runs from $242,000 to $252,000. Filing Form 8379, the Injured Spouse Allocation, means you can’t have your refund deposited into more than one account. Every account must be in the filer’s name.
 Setting Up the Split Before Filing
 She opens the IRA first. The IRS requires it to be established before she asks for direct deposit.
 She gets the routing and account numbers from the custodian (the firm holding the IRA) and asks whether to check “Checking” or “Savings,” since the wrong box can cause the deposit to be rejected.
 She tells the custodian which tax year the deposit is for.
 She fills in lines 1 through 3 of Form 8888 and checks the box on line 35a of Form 1040.
 She keeps the IRA amount within the 2026 limit of $7,500 ($8,600 for individuals age 50 or older), up from $7,000 ($8,000 for individuals age 50 or older) for 2025.
 What a Yearly Refund Deposit Could Grow To
 The IRS said on October 29, 2026, that the average refund this filing season rose 11%. That release doesn’t give a dollar figure for the average. As an assumption, take a $3,000 refund and put it away every year for 30 years with a 6% annual return. That would grow to about $237,175. Real returns vary, and this figure excludes fees and taxes.
 Other Splits the Same Form Allows
 She could send part of the refund to the IRA, part to savings, and the rest to checking. On a joint return, the instructions note that your spouse may get at least part of the refund, and each spouse may be able to contribute up to the limit. Each custodian still has to confirm it will accept the deposit. Buying savings bonds with a refund is no longer available. The IRS says that program has been discontinued.
 Deadlines That Can Undo the Contribution
 If she doesn’t tell the custodian the tax year, the custodian can assume the deposit is for the year you are filing your return for. That can push the money into the wrong year’s limit. The deposit also has to reach the account by the return’s due date, not including extensions.
 For 2025 contributions, that date was April 15, 2026. If it arrives late, it isn’t an IRA contribution for that year. She’d then have to file an amended return and cut back any IRA deduction and Saver’s Credit she claimed. About 90% of electronic filers got refunds in under 21 days this year, so a return filed in early April may not leave enough time.
 The deposit is still a contribution she has to report correctly on her return. Publication 590-A allows a filer to claim a traditional IRA contribution on a return before making the contribution. Also, no more than three refunds can go to a single account each year. Calling the IRA custodian before filing can confirm the account numbers, the correct box to check, and the deposit tax year.
